title: The New Girl Who Said Nothing

pages.text: The moving van arrived on a Saturday. It was the large kind, the kind that suggested a family who had not made any decisions about what to leave behind. It was at Flat 7B, which had been empty for three months. Chinasa was on her balcony eating an orange and watched the whole process with great attention.

image.note: Illustration: a large moving van at the entrance of an estate block, workers carrying furniture, Chinasa watching from a balcony above

pages.text: A girl emerged from the family car and stood on the pavement looking at the block. She was about eleven, with a long neck and the general air of someone cataloguing information. She looked at the block for about thirty seconds, then looked at Chinasa on the balcony above. Chinasa waved. The girl looked at her for a moment longer, then went inside.

'She waved back,' Chinasa reported to Isa later. 'She did not wave back,' Isa said. He had been watching from his own window. 'She looked at you and went inside.' 'That is very nearly the same thing,' Chinasa said.

Chinasa had a theory about new people, which was that they were all, underneath, waiting to be found interesting, and simply needed the right person to do the finding. She had appointed herself that person for the whole estate years ago, and had never once doubted her qualifications. So when the moving van pulled up at 7B and a girl climbed out of the car and stood looking up at the block, Chinasa was already leaning over her balcony rail, ready to begin.

The girl looked up. For a long moment she looked at Chinasa without any expression at all, the way you might look at a bird that had landed on a wire. Then she went inside. Chinasa remained on the balcony, orange forgotten in her hand, and revised her theory slightly. Some new people, it seemed, did not know yet that they were waiting to be found interesting. Those ones would simply require a little more work. Chinasa was not troubled. Chinasa was rarely troubled.

The new girl's name was Zara. The family were from Abuja but had been living in Kaduna for four years, and Zara had gone to school in Kaduna, and was starting at a new school in two weeks, and these facts were established in the first forty-eight hours by Chinasa's mother, who had the information-gathering speed of an experienced journalist and the generosity to share it freely.

image.note: Illustration: Chinasa's mother at the door of Flat 7B talking to Zara's mother, while both girls stand nearby not looking at each other

pages.text: Chinasa decided that Zara needed to be included. She invited her to play on the estate. Zara came and sat on the bench near the gate and watched. She smiled at the right moments. She did not join the game. 'Maybe she doesn't like that game,' Chinasa said. 'What game does she like?' 'We haven't established that yet,' Isa said, which Chinasa already knew.

Hanan brought her hair ribbon collection to show Zara, which was a significant gesture. Zara looked at each ribbon with the same level of careful attention and said she liked the blue one. 'Just one?' Hanan said. 'I would like to look at the others again before deciding,' Zara said. It was the longest sentence she had spoken in four days.

Nosa explained how the estate's water pump worked, using a diagram he drew on a scrap of paper. Zara listened to the whole explanation without interrupting, which Nosa found refreshing and slightly unusual.

Ini noticed the notebook on the third day. It was small, black, and always in Zara's left hand or visible through her bag. Zara wrote in it sometimes, briefly, when she thought no one was looking. She did not write while talking to people. She wrote immediately after.

image.note: Illustration: Zara sitting at the edge of a gathering of estate children, notebook slightly visible in her bag, pen in her hand

pages.text: Ini did not mention this to anyone. She mentioned very little to anyone. This was not rudeness. It was an editorial decision about what information other people were ready to receive.

On the fifth day, Ini sat next to Zara on the bench and did not say anything. Zara also said nothing. After seven minutes of this, Zara looked at Ini. 'You're not trying to make me talk,' she said. 'No,' Ini said. 'Everyone else is,' Zara said. 'Yes,' Ini said. 'Why?' Zara asked. 'Because they like you,' Ini said. 'They want you to like it here.'

Zara thought about this for a moment. 'I do like it here,' she said. 'I know,' Ini said. They sat quietly for another few minutes. 'Can I see the notebook?' Ini asked. Zara did not answer immediately. She looked at the notebook in her hand, then at Ini. Then she handed it over.

Ini had learned long ago that people showed you who they were if you let them, and that the trick was to stop talking long enough to notice. While the others tried harder and harder to draw Zara out, growing louder and more inventive, Ini did the opposite. She sat near Zara and said nothing, and watched, and let the silence be a place rather than a problem. It took five days, but on the fifth day the silence became a place Zara was willing to speak into.

What Ini had noticed was small and easy to miss: the notebook was always there, and Zara wrote in it only after something happened, never during. She did not write when spoken to. She wrote when she had watched. That was not shyness. Shyness hid from the world; this was the opposite, a person paying the world very close attention. Ini did not announce her conclusion. She simply sat down beside the right person and waited for the right moment, which is a skill of its own.

The notebook was full. Not full of notes. Full of story. Scenes from the estate, written in a close hand: Chinasa waving from the balcony, Hanan and her ribbon collection, Nosa's pump diagram, the children playing near the gate in the late afternoon light. Characters, written as characters: their small habits, their expressions, the way they moved.

image.note: Illustration: Ini reading the notebook, expression of genuine surprise and then pleasure

pages.text: Ini read two pages. She handed it back. She thought about what to say, which she always did before speaking. 'It's good,' she said. 'I know,' Zara said. 'You're not shy,' Ini said. 'No,' Zara said. 'Should I tell them that?' 'You probably should,' Ini said. 'Before Chinasa tries something worse than the ribbon collection.'

They told them. Chinasa was immediately interested in whether she was in it and in what it said about her. Nosa wanted to know if the pump diagram was accurate. Hanan asked whether the blue ribbon had been mentioned. Isa said that the methodology of observation without participation was, while effective for the purposes of fiction, somewhat antisocial.
'He says that,' Chinasa told Zara, 'but he watches everything from his window. He just uses different equipment.' Isa started to object and then didn't, which was as close as he came to agreeing.

Zara wrote in the notebook that evening for a long time. When she next joined the group at the bench near the gate, she still said less than most of them. But she laughed more, and the notebook was in her bag rather than in her hand, and Ini noticed this, and said nothing about it, which meant she thought it was good.
